---
applyTo: "app/controllers/**/*.rb,config/routes.rb"
---

# Controllers and routes

- Define RESTful actions in this order: `index`, `show`, `new`, `edit`, `create`, `update`, `destroy`. Leave out actions the resource does not need, but keep the rest in this order.
- Put a comment above each action with its route, in the Rails scaffold format with param names instead of example values, e.g. `# GET /posts/:id`.
- Only set instance variables in an action, or in a callback whose name starts with `set_`, e.g. `before_action :set_post` with `@post = Post.find(params[:id])` in `set_post`. You MUST NOT set them in other private methods, other callbacks, or memoised readers, e.g. `@post ||= Post.find(params[:id])`.
- You SHOULD NOT add a `helper_method` to a controller. Read instance variables in the view, and pass them to a partial as locals, e.g. `render "form", post: @post`.
- When a page shows a value read from another service, read it in the action or a `set_` callback, before the view renders. Call the service from a private method and assign the value to an instance variable, e.g. `@newsletter_stats = fetch_newsletter_stats` in `PostsController#show`, with `NewsletterClient.new.fetch_stats(@post.newsletter_id)` in `fetch_newsletter_stats`.
- When a template, a helper or a decorator's context needs a service value, a helper method MAY give it, but it only returns the value the action read, e.g. `helper_method :newsletter_stats` with a private `attr_reader :newsletter_stats`. You MUST NOT call the service from a helper method, e.g. `@newsletter_stats ||= NewsletterClient.new.fetch_stats(@post.newsletter_id)`.
- When a list shows a service value for each record, read them all in one call. You SHOULD give the view a helper method that looks up one record's value, e.g. `NewsletterClient.new.fetch_all_stats(@posts.filter_map(&:newsletter_id))` in `PostsController#index` with `helper_method :newsletter_stats_for`. You MUST NOT make one request for each record. For other options, see https://bmorrall.github.io/happy_rails/patterns/values-from-services/.
- In an action that changes a record, e.g. `create` or `update`, write the happy case first in an `if` and the failure case in the `else`, e.g. `if @post.save` then `redirect_to @post`, else the failure. When the action submits a form and uses the result, assign the result of `submit` in the `if` condition, in brackets, e.g. `if (post = @create_post_form.submit)` then `redirect_to post`. You MUST NOT assign it before the `if`. When the action doesn't use the result, you MUST NOT assign it, e.g. `if @archive_post_form.submit`.
- When an action fails and shows a form again, render it with `status: :unprocessable_content`, e.g. `render :new, status: :unprocessable_content` in `PostsController#create`. When there is no form to show, redirect instead, e.g. `redirect_to @post, alert: "Post could not be published."` in `Posts::PublicationsController#create`. On Rack before 3.1, use `status: :unprocessable_entity` instead, because `:unprocessable_content` raises there.
- Follow the app's existing flash message pattern in every controller. Read other controllers before writing a message, and copy their keys and wording, e.g. `notice: "Post was created."` if the app already uses `notice: "Comment was created."`. Use the same key for every success and the same key for every failure, e.g. `notice` and `alert`.
- Set a flash when an action redirects, e.g. `redirect_to @post, notice: "Post was updated."`. You MUST NOT set a flash when the action renders a form again, because the form's errors explain the failure.
- Put controllers for a nested resource in a module named after the parent controller, e.g. `Posts::CommentsController` in `app/controllers/posts/comments_controller.rb`. In `config/routes.rb`, put them in a `scope module: :posts` block inside `resources :posts`.
- Each nested module has a `BaseController`, e.g. `Posts::BaseController`, with a `before_action` that loads the parent record and checks the current user can see it, e.g. `set_post`. Nested controllers inherit from it and MUST NOT load the parent themselves. The base controller has no actions or routes.
- You MUST NOT let the base controller's check on the parent count as the nested action's own check. Each nested action still starts with its own authorisation check, e.g. `Posts::CommentsController#create` checks that the user can create a comment, not only that they can see `@post`.
- Avoid custom actions on resource controllers. Instead, add a new controller with a `create` action, using the nested module and `BaseController` pattern, e.g. `Posts::PublicationsController < BaseController` with `# POST /posts/:post_id/publication`, routed with `resource :publication, only: :create` inside `scope module: :posts`, instead of a `publish` action on `PostsController`.
- If a controller has custom actions, put them below the standard actions in alphabetical order, each with a route comment, e.g. `duplicate` then `preview` after `destroy`.
- Each controller has a default format for its use case (HTML for pages, JSON for APIs). Leave the default format out of route comments.
- When an action responds to another format, add a route comment with the format extension below the default route, e.g. `# GET /posts/:id.json`.
- When an action responds with a Turbo Stream, keep its HTML response too, and put `format.html` first in the `respond_to` block, e.g. `format.html { redirect_to @post }` before `format.turbo_stream` in `Posts::CommentsController#create`.
- You MUST NOT add a route comment for a Turbo Stream response, because Turbo uses the `Accept` header and the URL does not change.
- Nest a resource's params under its singular name, e.g. `post` for `PostsController` and `comment` for `Posts::CommentsController`.
- If the app uses Pundit, put the main app's permitted attributes in the policy and have `post_params` call Pundit, following the Pundit instructions. Use the `require` and `permit` rules below in apps without Pundit, and in controllers for other APIs, e.g. `Api::V1::PostsController`.
- Read params in a private method named after the resource, using `params.require` with the singular name and `permit` with an explicit list of attributes, e.g. `post_params` returns `params.require(:post).permit(:title, :body)`. You MUST NOT use `permit!` or permit a whole hash.
- When actions accept different attributes, replace the params method with one method per action, named with a `_for_<action>` suffix, e.g. `post_params_for_create` and `post_params_for_update`. You MUST NOT keep a plain `post_params` next to them.
- Write each action's permit list in full, even if attributes repeat, e.g. `post_params_for_create` permits `:title, :body, :slug` and `post_params_for_update` permits `:title, :body`. You MUST NOT build one list from another.
- Always use a gem or a built-in Rails authentication method to authenticate requests, e.g. `http_basic_authenticate_with`. You MUST NOT write a custom solution.
- You MUST NOT put the authentication check in individual controllers. `ApplicationController` runs it for every action. To make an action public, use `skip_before_action` with an `only:` list of just those actions, e.g. `skip_before_action :authenticate_user!, only: %i[index show]` in `PostsController`.
- Use Devise to authenticate users who sign in.
- When an API authenticates differently, put its check in the top-most controller that every API controller inherits from, e.g. `before_action :authenticate` in `Api::V1::BaseController`, with `Api::V1::PostsController < BaseController`.
- When you use a built-in Rails authentication method, keep usernames, passwords and tokens in Rails credentials or environment variables, not in code, e.g. `Rails.application.credentials.api_token`.
- Compare secrets with `ActiveSupport::SecurityUtils.secure_compare`, not `==`, e.g. `authenticate_or_request_with_http_token { |token, _options| ActiveSupport::SecurityUtils.secure_compare(token, Rails.application.credentials.api_token) }`.
- Handle each `rescue_from` with a private method passed with `with:`. Name the method `handle_` followed by the error class's name in snake case, keeping any `Error` suffix, e.g. `rescue_from ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound, with: :handle_record_not_found` and `rescue_from Pundit::NotAuthorizedError, with: :handle_not_authorized_error`. You MUST NOT pass a block to `rescue_from`.
- To handle an error differently in a subclass, override its `handle_` method and call `super` for the default.
- When a handler redirects, and a subclass or a controller that includes it might redirect elsewhere, redirect to the path from a private method named after the handler, with `after_` in place of `handle_` and `_path` on the end, e.g. `redirect_to after_not_authorized_error_path, alert: "You are not authorized to perform this action."` in `handle_not_authorized_error`. Override the path method, not the handler, and call `super` for the default. When only one controller uses the handler, redirect in the handler.
- Use `rescue_from` only for errors outside the app's normal flow, e.g. `ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound`. You MUST NOT use it for an outcome the app expects. Handle that in a form or a job.
- When an action the controller calls fails because another service failed, e.g. it returned a 500 or timed out, rescue the action's error class for that cause with `rescue_from`, and name the handler after the action and the error, e.g. `rescue_from Posts::SendNewsletter::ServiceError, with: :handle_send_newsletter_service_error`.
- When the action shares its errors with a group of actions through a base class, rescue the base class's error class for that cause, and name the handler after the base class, e.g. `rescue_from Posts::NewsletterAction::ServiceError, with: :handle_newsletter_action_service_error`.
- Always rescue the action's error class for the service failing itself as a catch-all, even when you also rescue its subclasses with their own handlers, e.g. `rescue_from Posts::SendNewsletter::ServiceError` alongside `rescue_from Posts::SendNewsletter::TimeoutError`.
- In a handler for another service failing, redirect with a fixed alert, e.g. `redirect_to post_path(@post), alert: "Newsletter could not be sent. Please try again later."`. You MUST NOT show the error's message, e.g. `alert: e.message`.
- In an API controller, render the action's error class for the service failing with `status: :bad_gateway` (502) and the alert's fixed text, e.g. `render json: { error: "Newsletter could not be sent. Please try again later." }, status: :bad_gateway`.
- When an API client needs another status for one cause, give the action a subclass of its error class for the service failing, e.g. `Posts::SendNewsletter::TimeoutError`, and rescue it with its own handler, e.g. `handle_send_newsletter_timeout_error`. Use `status: :gateway_timeout` (504) when the service took too long to reply, or `status: :service_unavailable` (503) when it can't be reached for now, e.g. it is down for maintenance.
- Declare a subclass's `rescue_from` after the one for its parent class, e.g. `Posts::SendNewsletter::TimeoutError` after `Posts::SendNewsletter::ServiceError`. Rails checks the last declared handler first.
- When more than one controller calls actions that share their errors, and they all inherit from the same `BaseController`, put the `rescue_from` and its handler in the base controller, e.g. `rescue_from Posts::NewsletterAction::ServiceError, with: :handle_newsletter_action_service_error` in `Posts::BaseController` for `Posts::PublicNewslettersController` and `Posts::PrivateNewslettersController`. In the handler, redirect to the parent record, e.g. `redirect_to post_path(@post)`.
- When the controllers that call actions that share their errors don't share a base controller, put the `rescue_from` and its handler in a concern named after the base class, ending in `ErrorHandling`, e.g. `NewsletterActionErrorHandling` in `app/controllers/concerns/newsletter_action_error_handling.rb` for `PostsController` and `Posts::PrivateNewslettersController`. Include it in each controller that calls the group's actions.
- In an error handling concern, redirect to the handler's `after_` path method, and return `root_path` from it, e.g. `redirect_to after_newsletter_action_service_error_path, alert: "Newsletter could not be sent. Please try again later."` with `def after_newsletter_action_service_error_path` returning `root_path`.
- In each controller that includes an error handling concern, you SHOULD override its `after_` path method to go back to the record the user was working on, e.g. `def after_newsletter_action_service_error_path` returning `post_path(@post)` in `PostsController`.
- For API controllers, write a separate error handling concern that renders a fixed response with `status: :bad_gateway`, e.g. `Api::NewsletterActionErrorHandling` in `app/controllers/concerns/api/newsletter_action_error_handling.rb`.
- Use Pundit to authorise requests. Follow the Pundit instructions for how to write each check.
- Start every action with an authorisation check on its first line, before it loads more data, changes a record or renders anything, e.g. the check comes before `@post.update(post_params)` in `update`.
- Leave a blank line after the authorisation check, unless it is the only line in the action, e.g. a blank line between the check and `@post.update(post_params)` in `update`.
- You MUST NOT set up the default authorisation check in individual controllers. `ApplicationController` already requires it.
- When an action needs no authorisation check, opt out on the action's first line, e.g. in `PagesController#about`. You MUST NOT opt out for the whole controller, because that also covers actions added later.
- Keep routes RESTful. Model a custom action as a resource of its own whenever you can.
- Give every `resources` and `resource` call an `only:` list that matches the controller's actions, e.g. `resources :posts, only: %i[index show]`. You MUST NOT use `except:`. Leave `only:` off only when the controller has all seven standard actions.
- Declare routes with `resources`, `resource`, `namespace` and `root`. You MUST NOT write a path by hand, e.g. `get "posts/:id/preview", to: "posts#preview"`. Route a custom action in a `member` or `collection` block, e.g. `member { get :preview }` inside `resources :posts`.
- Use a singular `resource` when there is only one of something, e.g. `resource :profile, only: %i[show edit update]` with `# GET /profile`. Still name the controller in the plural, e.g. `ProfilesController`, not `ProfileController`.
- Use `namespace` when both the URL and the controller module change, e.g. `namespace :api` and `namespace :v1` for `Api::V1::PostsController` with `# GET /api/v1/posts`. Use `scope module:` when only the module changes, e.g. nested resources.
- Nest resources one level deep at most. You MUST NOT use `shallow: true`.
- Instead of shallow routes, declare the actions on a single nested record as a top-level resource, e.g. `resources :comments, only: %i[index new create]` inside `scope module: :posts`, and `resources :comments, only: %i[show edit update destroy]` at the top level, routed to `CommentsController` with `# GET /comments/:id`.
- Build links and redirects with path helpers or records, e.g. `post_path(@post)` or `redirect_to @post`. You MUST NOT write a URL as a string.
